items.title: Behind the Scenes at My First Comic Con
items.summary: Attending my very first MCM London Comic Con as press on October 23 and 24 was an absolute dream.
items.content_html:
Attending my very first MCM London Comic Con as press on October 23 and 24 was an absolute dream. Representing Tarot Interviews at ExCeL London, I spent two whirlwind days soaking in the glorious nerdery vibes, recording 30 fantastic interviews, snapping 150 photos, and clocking over 40,000 steps. Oh, and far too many snacks to power me through.

The sheer creativity on display was incredible. From the breathtaking costumes that some people had taken a year or more to make, to the brilliant writers, illustrators, and artists showcasing their craft, inspiration was everywhere. I even got to meet an artist that created some of my favourite childhood comic strips.

I spent most of my time wandering through Artists’ Alley and Writers’ Block, chatting with creators for an upcoming episode of Tarot Interviews. There’s nothing quite like the joy of stumbling across unique projects and passionate voices you might never have discovered otherwise.

Of course, I couldn't resist capturing some of the stunning cosplay and yes, TAROTRON 2000 made a few friends too.

If you want a sneak peek at the visual madness, I’ve already shared a generous batch of photos over on Instagram - head to @finbarre and @tarotron2000

Right now, I’m editing all the audio and editing together our special MCM episode, which will be landing on Spotify and Apple Podcasts soon. I’ll be sharing direct links to all the featured creators once it goes live so you can support their work.

A massive, heartfelt thank you to the MCM press team for having me, and an even bigger thank you to everyone who shared a story, posed for a picture, or just stopped to say hello. You made my first-ever Comic Con experience special, you fabulous folks.

A huge thank you to everyone who stopped to chat, posed for a photograph or agreed to be interviewed. It was a pleasure meeting you all.

items.title: Fridays in London: MCM, Tate Britain and the Society of Antiquaries
items.summary: October and November are shaping up to be a busy few weeks, with three Friday appearances in London involving…
items.content_html:
October and November are shaping up to be a busy few weeks, with three Friday appearances in London involving podcasting, tarot history and research.

23 October 2026: MCM London

I’ll be at MCM London at ExCeL with press access, recording material for the Tarot Interviews podcast.

Tarot Interviews uses randomly drawn tarot cards to generate questions, creating conversations that can move in directions neither guest nor interviewer can predict in advance. At MCM, I’ll be taking the format into the convention itself and recording with guests on site.

30 October 2026: Tate Britain

A week later, I’ll be speaking at Tate Britain on:

“The Pre-Raphaelites and Pixie: Pamela Colman Smith and the Art of Tarot”

The talk looks at Pamela Colman Smith, the artist behind the imagery of the Rider-Waite-Smith tarot, in the context of her artistic life and the visual culture surrounding her work.

6 November 2026: Society of Antiquaries of London

The following Friday I’ll be at Burlington House for the Society of Antiquaries of London, speaking on:

“The Afterlife of a Pack: The Rider-Waite-Smith Tarot in Print and Use”

This talk turns from the creation of the deck to what happened afterwards, looking at the Rider-Waite-Smith tarot as a printed object that has been reproduced, customised and used for more than a century.

If you’re attending any of them, come and say hello!

23 October · MCM London · ExCeL London
30 October · Tate Britain
6 November · Society of Antiquaries of London · Burlington House

items.title: I Built a Haunted Little Tarot Robot
items.summary: TAROTRON 2000 is a pocket-sized tarot machine I’ve been developing as an experiment in creative technology. Built using Arduino…
items.content_html:
TAROTRON 2000 is a pocket-sized tarot machine I’ve been developing as an experiment in creative technology.

Built using Arduino and an M5StickS3, the prototype runs on a tiny computer with its own screen, speaker and controls. Give it a command and it randomly selects a Rider-Waite-Smith tarot card, displays the card and its meaning, and talks about what it has chosen.

It has rather more personality than was strictly necessary.

The idea grew out of several strands of my work. I’ve spent more than thirty years working with tarot, built CardMeanings.com as a reference to the 78 Rider-Waite-Smith cards, and I really wanted a new gadget to bring to events. I had been searching on eBay for an 80s electronic tarot toy, only to realise I could make one myself.

The current prototype can select cards, display their meanings, speak, make noises, change its behaviour and occasionally say things it probably shouldn't via a special "Cursed Mode".

I’m now using TAROTRON 2000 to produce a short daily card draw while continuing to experiment with what else this peculiar little machine can do.

If you're curious, follow this silliness at

https://www.youtube.com/@TAROTRON2000
https://www.instagram.com/tarotron2000
https://www.tiktok.com/@tarotron2000

items.title: What Tarot Cards Have Taught Me About Interviewing
items.summary: I recently wrote for Journalism.co.uk about what using randomly selected tarot cards has taught me about interviewing. In Tarot…
items.content_html:
I recently wrote for Journalism.co.uk about what using randomly selected tarot cards has taught me about interviewing.

In Tarot Interviews and Tarot DMs, I use three randomly selected cards to shape three questions. Neither I nor the guest knows exactly where the conversation will go.

The piece looks at what introducing chance can do to an interview, how it can get beyond rehearsed answers, and why giving up a little editorial control can sometimes produce a more interesting conversation.

It sets out the technique I have pioneered as aleatory journalism: using chance, structured constraints and unexpected prompts as tools within the journalistic process.

Read: What using tarot cards as random prompts has taught me about interviews

Published by Journalism.co.uk, September 2026.

items.title: Valuing the Tarot Interviews Catalog
items.summary: When you build something entirely by hand and without a safety net, you have to remind yourself of the…
items.content_html:
When you build something entirely by hand and without a safety net, you have to remind yourself of the project's worth.

I recently sat down to map out the true editorial media value across every single podcast episode and written feature across Tarot Interviews and Tarot DMs.

Across more than 70 generous contributions, I weighed three things: what it would cost to commercially produce this work, the real effort of securing each guest, and the actual reach of the audience that showed up to listen and read.

The archive at a glance

  • Combined Output: £57,226 (conservative range: £31,712 to £95,155)
  • Tarot Interviews: £20,451
  • Tarot DMs: £36,775

This figure represents the raw craft, hours, and distribution effort required to bring this entire archive into the world.

The people who inhabit this space make it so special. Literary powerhouses like Joanne Harris, Adrian Tchaikovsky, and Lauren Beukes share the exact same floor space with underground musicians, visual artists, academics, stage performers, and festival regulars. Tarot DMs carried a massive share of this footprint, with individual features touching anywhere between 4,000 and 60,000 readers.

What we give back to our guests

  • Per Guest Feature: £829 avg in equivalent promotional and editorial value
  • Weekly Output (4 features a week): £3,316
  • Monthly Impact: £14,369
  • Annual Impact: £172,432

Every person who sits down for an interview receives a permanent piece of original media that stays online, alongside the advertising-equivalent weight of its audience reach.

Putting concrete numbers to this work gives us an undeniable baseline for future conversations about funding, sponsorship, and long-term partnerships.

Counting all of this up makes me wonder where the Tarot Interviews project will be next year.

items.title: Tarot Interviews Joins Podcasting’s 1%

items.content_html:
Only 1% of podcasts launched are estimated to reach break-even or better.

My Tarot Interviews podcast has now done that in eighteen months, recovering its original equipment costs.

Now, this does not include my time, but it is still a milestone for an independently produced podcast using an experimental format in a specialist field.

Thank you to everyone who helped it get here!

Take a listen by visiting https://tarotinterviews.com

items.title: Previous Guests
items.summary: It is not every day you get to pause and reflect on how far a creative project has come,…
items.content_html:
It is not every day you get to pause and reflect on how far a creative project has come, but today is one of those days! 

I recently sat down to update the guest directory for my projects, Tarot Interviews and Tarot DMs, and realized we’ve hit a pretty wonderful milestone: we have officially featured over 70 guests and contributors. For those new to the project, the premise is simple but revealing: a three-card, three-question format used to interview writers, artists, musicians, and cultural figures.

Over the course of 70+ interviews, this format has adapted into two spaces:

  • Tarot Interviews: A traditional audio podcast format.
  • Tarot DMs: Written interviews conducted entirely through messaging apps.

The most rewarding part of this journey has been the sheer diversity of the people who have agreed to sit down (or log on) and pull cards with me. I have spoken with internationally bestselling authors like Joanne Harris and Adrian Tchaikovsky, brilliant narrative designers, historians, and musicians. Tarot Interviews has even taken the format on the road, interviewing festival crew members, artisan blacksmiths, and performers right in the middle of muddy fields!

A huge thank you to all the creative minds who have trusted me with their time and their stories.

If you want to see the full, newly updated list of guests, or check out the format for yourself, you can find the directory over on https://tarotinterviews.com/previous-guests

items.title: Free 2026 Community Partner Spots
items.summary: Tarot Interviews is opening a small number of free community partner spots for tarot, folklore, heritage, arts and culture…
items.content_html:
Tarot Interviews is opening a small number of free community partner spots for tarot, folklore, heritage, arts and culture organizations.

Selected partners can share a finished 30 second audio message with Tarot Interviews listeners. There is no fee. In return, I ask partners to help spread the word with an Instagram follow, social post, tag or link where possible.

UK-based projects, podcasts and cultural or heritage work may be prioritised, but international submissions are very welcome.

Please send finished audio only, as a WAV or high quality MP3.

Spots are limited and all submissions will be reviewed before approval.
